newsitem.title: MEXICO: Contenders line up for key Mexico mayor's job.
newsitem.headline: Contenders line up for key Mexico mayor's job.

text.p: Leading contenders emerged on Friday for a job many see as the second most important after the president's -- to be the first elected mayor of Mexico's huge, sprawling metropolis.

Mexico City will elect a mayor in July under changes enacted by President Ernesto Zedillo to foster greater democracy. The job carries huge political and symbolic weight in a highly centralized country.
Hitherto the capital has been governed by a presidential nominee and member of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

The PRI on Thursday opened nominations for candidates and newspapers on Friday mentioned three possible names, including the former governor of Mexico state Alfredo del Mazo, who is loosely linked to party hardliners.
But insiders believed Mexico City chief prosecutor Jose Antonio Gonzalez Fernandez may well be Zedillo's choice.
Little known until recently, Gonzalez Fernandez entered the limelight recently with a series of high-profile news conferences and appearances accompanied by Zedillo.
Party officials said the PRI would decide its candidate at a convention on Feb. 19, but few expect much real competition in a party where the "spontaneous emergence of a unity candidate" is the norm.
Whoever is chosen by the PRI faces an uphill struggle.
Almost all recent opinion polls show the PRI in second or third place in the capital behind the conservative National Action Party (PAN), the No. 2 political force nationwide.
One well-respected pollster, Vicente Licona of Indemerc/Louis Harris, said his surveys indicated the PRI cannot win no matter who they run or who the oppposition runs.
Mexicans, he said, were too angry about rising violent crime, pollution and official corruption to give the long-ruling PRI another chance.

That view has gained ground, analysts said, because some of the PRI's best-known names, such as ambassador to Washington Jesus Silva Herzog or Senate leader Fernando Ortiz Arana, made clear they did not want to run.
The PAN had two candidates vying for its nomination, with former party president Carlos Castillo Peraza the front runner.
PAN delegates will vote on their candidate at a special convention on March 2 but other candidates could emerge.

Party militants hoped former PAN presidential candidate Diego Fernandez de Cevallos -- a fiery orator showed by polls to be the PAN's strongest candidate -- will reconsider his insistence on not running.
On the left, the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), was likely to choose between two-time presidential candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, and ex-leader Porfirio Munoz Ledo.
Both were former PRI politicians, but polls indicated Cardenas would have a better chance of winning.
